attempt: Items (1)-(5) impose a name-resolution outcome (program C cannot refer to a local name; C reaches B's global name) that no row states.
reason: The items are a worked example of rows 1985-GR-X.1.3.8.2-1..3: the set of names is B's names plus the global names of A and its containers, so a name local in both A and B is outside C's set (item 3) and a global in B or in A is in it (items 4, 5); item 2 is X.1.3.8.2-3a; item 1's one-object rule for external objects is the 6.2.2.2 prose 'References to an external object ... are always to the same object'.
quoted: program C cannot refer to that name

attempt: Items (1)-(4) fix which program a call of DUPLICATE-NAME activates; the precedence of a contained over a separately compiled program might be stated nowhere.
reason: 1985-GR-X.5.2.4-4 states the mechanism: a directly contained program of the same name is called, else a common program of an enclosing program unless the caller is inside it, else the separately compiled program. Each of items (1)-(4) is an instance (2a common, 2b not common, 3 caller inside the contained program, 4 any other caller); visibility is 1985-SR-X.1.3.8.1-1..3 and 1985-SR-II.6.4.1.2-1..4.
quoted: the program called is the separately compiled program named DUPLICATE-NAME

attempt: The three circumstances in which two programs share data might add a condition the rows omit.
reason: 1985-GR-X.1.3.6-1, -2 and -3 are the same three sentences word for word (the 'See page II-19' pointer is the only addition). The block adds no condition.
quoted: establishes a common data item

attempt: The two circumstances for sharing file connectors might differ from the rows in scope.
reason: 1985-GR-X.1.3.7-1 and -2 state both sentences word for word. The following 6.5 intro sentence is a description of intra-program communication with no verbal form.
quoted: An external file connector may be referenced from any program which describes that file connector

attempt: The paragraph after the list says the PERFORM restrictions apply equally to SORT/MERGE input-output procedures and that declaratives have stricter ones; no row states that.
reason: The four list items are bare names of constructs, but the text after them is a rule: 'the restrictions on the PERFORM statement apply equally to input-output procedures' and 'Stricter restrictions, than those for the PERFORM statement, apply to declarative procedures'. Section II is outside the unit campaign (Sections IV, VI-XVI, A), so no unit holds it. Rows XI.4.4.4-7/-10 and XI.4.1.4-8 give only the range; PERFORM's nesting rule 1985-GR-VI.6.21.4-14 is stated for PERFORM alone. No row carries the equal-application rule or the declaratives sentence.
quoted: the restrictions on the PERFORM statement apply equally to input-output procedures

attempt: The closing paragraph says the user must specify symbolic names known to the MCS and defines queues before execution.
reason: 1985-GR-XIV.2.2.4-4 requires the symbolic names to follow system-name formation and 'have been previously defined to the message control system'. The three list items describe the MCS's functions (interface, line discipline, device-dependent tasks), an environment description with no obligation on a program or compiler.
quoted: The COBOL user must specify in his COBOL program symbolic names which are known to the message control system

attempt: Pass 3 (kb/Work PB6051 p114-1) redrew Figure 1; the redrawn routing of queues to devices, or the two numbered lists, might impose a rule no catalog row states.
reason: Every list item restates a statement whose rows define its effect: ACCEPT MESSAGE COUNT 1985-GR-XIV.3.1.4-1; DISABLE 1985-GR-XIV.3.2.1-p1, 3.2.4-1, 3.2.4-6; ENABLE 1985-GR-XIV.3.3.1-p1, 3.3.4-1, 3.3.4-5; RECEIVE 1985-GR-XIV.3.5.4-1; SEND to one or more queues 1985-GR-XIV.3.6.4-6 and the destination table of 1985-GR-XIV.2.2.4-16. The figure is one example of the queue and device connections and the clause gives no routing rule for it, so the redraw adds no obligation.
quoted: The COBOL source program uses three statements to control the interface with the message control system
refuter: cobol-refuter pb6051 pass 3 (II.7.3 re-refuted after the Figure 1 redraw)

attempt: The three methods might impose a way a scheduled program must test for messages.
reason: The lead-in says the program 'can use' three methods; they are the statements ACCEPT MESSAGE COUNT and RECEIVE with and without NO DATA, whose rules are 1985-GR-XIV.3.1.4-1 and 1985-GR-XIV.3.5.4-5. Permissive, no obligation.
quoted: scheduled for execution through the normal means available

attempt: Item (1) says one CD 'must contain' FOR INITIAL INPUT or FOR INITIAL I-O.
reason: The lead-in makes the list 'one technique that may be used'; the 'must' is a precondition of the technique, not of a program. The binding CD rules for the INITIAL clause are in XIV.2.2 (1985-GR-XIV.2.2.4-6 and the clause rules).
quoted: the following is one technique that may be used

attempt: The two reasons might say when output is held or an input queue must be enabled.
reason: Both items are 'common reasons' a message stays in an output queue after the program ends; the enable condition is ENABLE/DISABLE (1985-GR-XIV.3.3.4-2, XIV.3.2.4-3). Descriptive only.
quoted: Two common reasons for this occurrence are

attempt: The text after the figure says what is returned when sub-queue levels are omitted and that both queue and sub-queue names must be given to read a given sub-queue.
reason: 1985-GR-XIV.2.2.4-5 states that when a level is specified all higher levels must be, that the MCS picks the next message when fewer levels are given, and that the names of all levels are returned. The alphabetical choice and the four RECEIVE examples sit under 'Let us assume that the MCS operates under the following queueing algorithm', an assumption and an illustration.
quoted: If the COBOL programmer wishes to access the next message in a queue

attempt: The glossary states a rule on every general format: 'integer' must be an unsigned nonzero numeric integer literal unless a rule allows otherwise.
reason: The two numbered lists are definitions (At End Condition, Qualifier, Text Word) whose rules sit in READ, RETURN and SEARCH. But the clause also holds sentences with must: under Integer, 'integer must be a numeric literal which is an integer, and it must be neither signed nor zero unless explicitly allowed'; Data-Name, 'must not be reference-modified, subscripted, or qualified unless specifically permitted'; Variable Occurrence Data Item, 'must contain an OCCURS DEPENDING ON clause'. A grep of all 2,275 rows finds no row for the first two; Section III is outside the unit campaign, so no unit holds them.
quoted: Where the term 'integer' appears in the general formats, integer must be a numeric literal which is an integer

attempt: The four conditions might bind implementor-added reserved words (none starting with a digit, X, Y or Z).
reason: The items state properties of the standard's own list (IV-45) and carry no verbal form of obligation ('do not begin'). Section 1.5 says an implementation may extend the list of reserved words and still meet the requirements; the binding sentence is the paragraph's lead ('must not appear ... as user-defined words'), carried by 1985-SR-IV.4.2.2.1-1.
quoted: Reserved words do not contain two or more contiguous hyphens

attempt: The two features might state a file-description obligation.
reason: 'include such features as' makes the list illustrative; the items are noun phrases ('The grouping of logical records...', 'The means by which the file can be identified'). The clause has no sentence after the list.
quoted: The grouping of logical records within the physical limitations of the file medium

attempt: The list might define the four kinds of specification.
reason: It names the titles of 4.4.1-4.4.4 that follow, each its own clause; a table of contents with no sentence of its own.
quoted: There are four types of explicit and implicit specifications

attempt: The three sentences of the Function paragraph might impose what SET may do.
reason: They summarise formats 1-3 of SET, whose requirements are the SR and GR of VI.6.23.3 and VI.6.23.4 (index setting, external switches, conditional variables). A Function paragraph has no verbal form.
quoted: The SET statement establishes reference points for table handling operations

attempt: The three items might impose what the tables must contain.
reason: The items state what the presentation rules tables specify; the requirements are the rows 1985-GR-XIII.3.10.6-1 to XIII.3.10.10-4. The block has no tail after the list.
quoted: The permissible combinations of LINE NUMBER and NEXT GROUP clauses

attempt: The text says no upper/lower limit rule or fit test rule exists without a PAGE clause and that fit tests apply only to body groups.
reason: 1985-GR-XIII.3.8.4-3 gives the single page of indefinite length without a PAGE clause; fit test rules are 1985-GR-XIII.3.10.8-3 (the only body group row) and the first-print-line, next-group and LINE-COUNTER rules are rows 3.10.6 to 3.10.10; the five items only say what each column of the tables is for. 3.10.2's own paragraphs are units of the clause.
quoted: even for body groups there are no fit test rules when the PAGE clause is omitted

attempt: Items (1)-(3) define A, R and NP, the codes of column 1 of every presentation rules table; no row defines them.
reason: They are not an index: each defines the meaning of a table code ('A' is one or more absolute LINE NUMBER clauses none with NEXT PAGE, in consecutive order; 'R' relative ones; 'NP' absolute ones with NEXT PAGE in the first and only the first clause) and the closing sentence defines two abbreviations together. Rows XIII.3.10.6 to XIII.3.10.10 apply only to the combination named by column 1, so conformance to a table row depends on these definitions. A grep of the catalog for "letter 'A' represents" finds no row. Under IV.3.2 a general rule defines the meaning of an element, so these are rules. List items are no units (rule_catalog_1985.units), so nothing else holds them.
quoted: The letter 'A' represents one or more absolute LINE NUMBER clauses

attempt: Item (3) says sections that communicate frequently should get the same segment-number.
reason: Every item is guidance: 'normally classified', 'Generally, the more frequently...', 'should be given'. 'Should' is advisory in the 1985 text; the segment-number rules proper are in XVI.1.6 onward (the lead-in points to XVI-7).
quoted: Sections which frequently communicate with one another should be given the same segment-numbers

attempt: Item (9) says an implementor must handle 50 levels of qualification; no row states that capacity.
reason: The list summarises changes and most items restate a module rule, but not all: item (9) 'An implementor must provide the capability to handle 50 levels of qualification. Five levels of qualification were required in second Standard COBOL.' has no row. A regex over the 2,275 rows (levels of qualification, 50 qualifiers, qualification near 50) returns nothing, and the module text for qualification (IV.4.3.8.4) states no number. The only other places are the Section I level tables ('50 qualifiers', N | X), which are tables and no rows. The reader's 'each item describes a change' fails for (9).

attempt: Some of the 42 changes might state a requirement no module rule does.
reason: Sampled about 10 items against the rows and module text: (1) 1985-GR-IV.4.2.2.2.3-L2.3; (6) 1985-SR-VII.4.3.3-3; (10) the Linkage rule 'must not contain a REDEFINES clause' (X.5.2.3 text); (12) 1985-GR-VI.6.3.4-1; (24) 1985-SR-XI.2.5.3-1 and -4; (31) 1985-GR-VI.6.24.4-2; (32) VI.6.24.4-3; (17) VI.4.3.4-5; (14) X.5.3.4-10; (8) OCCURS text. All stated at their module. Justification paragraphs are history. Not every item was checked; no counterexample found.

attempt: The bullet says a conforming implementation is required to support obsolete elements, a requirement.
reason: The same sentence, word for word, is in 1.5.2.3 ('A conforming implementation of Standard COBOL is required to support obsolete language elements of the subset and levels...'), and the obsolescence of each element is stated at the element's own rules. The list items name each element with a justification.

attempt: An item might add an implementor duty (alignment, external switch scope).
reason: Every item ends in a '(See ...)' pointer to the rule that holds the duty (IV.4.2.2.1.2, IV.4.3.4, IV.4.3.5, IV.4.5), e.g. 'Rules for the formation of a system-name are defined by the implementor'; nothing in the sample is absent from the pointed rule. An index.

attempt: Item (4) says the operating system ignores positioning when not applicable.
reason: Row 1985-GR-VI.6.10.4-10 (DISPLAY) states the positioning rule; the other items state the dependence of an element on a device type, a hardware-dependence index with the module level in brackets.

attempt: An undefined-result item might state a requirement the pointed rule lacks.
